result.summary: After sailing from Troy, Hercules fights a string of wars: at Cos, against Augeas and the Molionides in Elis, at Pylus, and in Lacedaemon. He then fathers many children, marries Deianira, kills Nessus, and conquers more lands. Deianira's love charm poisons him, he dies on a pyre on Mount Oeta and becomes immortal. The chapter ends with long lists of his sons.

scenes.title: Storms and the siege of Cos
scenes.summary: Hera's storms strike Hercules, and Zeus hangs her from Olympus. Hercules takes Cos, kills Eurypylus, and then helps the gods against the giants at Phlegra.
scenes.stakes: Hercules faces storms, a stone barrage and a wound in battle, but is saved by Zeus.

scenes.title: War against Augeas in Elis
scenes.summary: Hercules marches on Augeas, is stalled by illness and the Molionides, then kills them and takes Elis. He installs Phyleus and founds the Olympian games.
scenes.stakes: Hercules' army is attacked while he is sick; he risks defeat.

scenes.title: Pylus and Lacedaemon campaigns
scenes.summary: Hercules destroys Pylus, sparing Nestor, and wounds Hades. He attacks Hippocoon and his sons, using the Gorgon's hair at Tegea, and restores Tyndareus.
scenes.stakes: Hercules fights shape-shifting and divine foes and loses his brother Iphicles.

scenes.title: Auge and Telephus
scenes.summary: Hercules seduces Auge at Tegea. Her son Telephus is exposed, suckled by a doe, and she is sent abroad to Teuthras.
scenes.stakes: Auge and her baby face exposure and exile.

scenes.title: Deianira, Achelous and Nessus
scenes.summary: Hercules wins Deianira by defeating Achelous, fathers children, and accidentally kills a boy. In exile he shoots Nessus, who gives Deianira a false love charm.
scenes.stakes: Hercules faces exile for the killing, and Deianira is threatened by Nessus.

scenes.title: Wars around Trachis and Oechalia
scenes.summary: Hercules fights for Aegimius, kills Cycnus, Amyntor and others, and sacks Oechalia, taking Iole captive. He builds an altar at Cenaeum.
scenes.stakes: Hercules risks his life in repeated combat to punish enemies.

scenes.title: The poisoned tunic and apotheosis
scenes.summary: Deianira smears the tunic with Nessus' blood, and it burns Hercules. She hangs herself; Hercules dies on a pyre at Oeta, is lifted to heaven, and marries Hebe.
scenes.stakes: Hercules suffers agonizing poison and death; Deianira loses her husband and her life.

scenes.title: Hercules' many sons
scenes.summary: Lists of the sons of Hercules by the daughters of Thespius and by other women.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic-style name for the twin sons Eurytus and Cteatus, born of Molione.

notable_quotes.reason: Marks Hercules' apotheosis, carried to heaven by a cloud and thunder.
The poisoned tunic of Nessus brings Hercules' agonizing end.

analysis.text: Hercules' violence and desire carry consequences: his killings, seductions and debts lead to exile, Nessus' trap and death, before reward as a god.
The long genealogies link Hercules to many Greek peoples and royal houses, such as Croesus' family, serving as legitimizing ancestry and colonial claims, like the Sardinian colony.

legacy.text: The shirt of Nessus became a proverbial phrase for a fatal gift, and Sophocles' Women of Trachis dramatizes Hercules' death.
Hercules' founding of the Olympian games gave a mythical origin for the Greek festival.

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus, but is now thought to date from the 1st or 2nd century AD.

language_notes.text: Hera's hostility toward Hercules runs through his legend; she sends storms in revenge, and Zeus punishes her by suspending her from the sky, with weights on her feet in some versions.
"Piratical squadron" means a fleet of pirate ships; the Coans took his arrival for a raid.
The war on the giants at Phlegra was a battle in which the gods needed a mortal's help to defeat the giants, as fate had decreed.
"Two men joined in one" describes the Molionides as conjoined twins, a double body with two heads and four arms and legs.
"Molionides" is a patronymic: the sons of Molione, namely Eurytus and Cteatus.
"Apprized" is an old spelling of "apprised", meaning informed.
The Olympian games were the great festival at Olympia in Elis, here traced to Hercules as founder.
"Change his shape": Periclymenus had a gift from Poseidon to transform himself, into an eagle, bee or serpent in some tellings, to evade enemies.
Gerenians: people of Gerenia, a town in Messenia, where Nestor was raised and hence called "Gerenian" in epic.
"Did not look before her": she must not look straight ahead at the lock's effect; the Gorgon's hair carried petrifying, terrifying power.
"Debauched" here means seduced or violated; the text gives no sense of consent.
"Exposed" means left outdoors to die, a common ancient practice for unwanted infants.
"Cast her fawn": the doe had recently given birth, so she had milk. The name Telephus is often linked to the Greek for doe (elaphos).
"Wooed" means courted in order to marry; here the courtship becomes a contest with a rival suitor.
The horn of Amalthea is the cornucopia, the "horn of plenty", a famous symbol of abundance.
"Endeavored" is a garbled rendering of a boy's name (the boy is named Eunomus in other accounts). The text here is corrupt, so treat the word as a name.
"In accordance with the law" refers to the custom that a killer, even an accidental one, went into exile to purify himself.
A centaur is a creature with a man's upper body and a horse's body. Nessus uses his strength to ferry travelers across the river.
"Barb" means the arrowhead, which was poisoned with the Hydra's venom. This is why Nessus's blood becomes a deadly charm.
"In lack of food" means short of food; Hercules, hungry, takes a bullock from a passing farmer.
"Being besieged" refers to Aegimius, who was under siege by the Lapiths, not Hercules.
"Wanton" here means insolent and lawless, giving the reason for the king's killing.
"Closing with him" means engaging him in close combat.
"To wit" is an archaic phrase meaning "namely", introducing the list of the fallen.
The altar of "Cenaean Zeus" honors Zeus (Jove) at Cenaeum. This sets up the sacrifice and the fatal robe sent by Deianira.
"Damsel" is an archaic word for a young unmarried woman; here it refers to Iole, whom Hercules desired.
Nessus the centaur, dying from Hercules' arrow, told Deianira his blood would work as a love-charm. It was really poisoned by the hydra's venom.
The hydra's poison was on Hercules' arrows, which had wounded Nessus; it thus returns through the blood to destroy Hercules.
"Wafted" means carried gently through the air.
"To wit" is an old formula meaning "that is to say"; it introduces the list that follows.

context_notes.text: Poseidon is the god of the sea; many heroes and kings in Greek myth are called his sons.
Athena, goddess of wisdom and war, often aids Hercules.
Augeas, king of Elis, is the owner of the filthy stables Hercules cleaned as a labour, and he refused payment.
Phyleus was Augeas' son who had taken Hercules' side over the unpaid wages and was exiled by his father.
Hades, god of the dead, was said to be wounded by Hercules at Pylus; the gods occasionally fought in mortal wars.
Hippocoon had seized Sparta (Lacedaemon) from his half-brother Tyndareus; Hercules' campaign is partly a restoration of the rightful king.
Athena (the Greek goddess of war and wisdom) gave the Gorgon Medusa's hair; Hercules uses it as a protective talisman for Tegea.
Nauplius, son of Poseidon, was a seafarer; Aleus uses him to get rid of Auge, who ended up in Mysia with Teuthras.
Achelous was a river god who could change shape. He is often shown as a bull, and the broken horn explains a mythical origin for the cornucopia.
Thespius was a king whose fifty daughters each bore a son to Hercules. Here Hercules arranges where the sons will go.
Deianira later uses this "charm" on Hercules's shirt, which leads to his death. The poisoned blood is the key to his end.
The Dorians were a Greek people; Aegimius is their legendary ancestral king, whose descendants were later linked with Hercules' sons.
Ares (the Greek war god) was said to be Cycnus' father, which makes the duel a clash with a divine son.
Eurytus of Oechalia had refused Hercules his daughter Iole despite winning her in an archery contest, so Hercules sought revenge.
Lichas is Hercules' herald and servant; the raiment he fetches leads to the poisoned robe and Hercules' death.
Lichas was the herald who brought Deianira's tunic to Hercules; he was an innocent messenger, yet bears the first violence.
Oeta is a mountain in central Greece, traditionally the place of Hercules' death on the pyre.
Hebe was goddess of youth. Hera had long persecuted Hercules, so their reconciliation marks his acceptance among the gods.
Thespius, king of Thespiae, had fifty daughters. Hercules fathered children by them in a single night's stay, according to the tradition.

literary_notes.text: Zeus's sudden rescue removes Hercules from danger, showing the hero's divine parentage and protection.
The doubled body and extraordinary strength mark the Molionides as formidable, monstrous rivals worthy of Hercules.
The Molionides, who attacked a sick Hercules in a broken truce, are themselves ambushed while attending a sacred festival.
Sparing young Nestor prepares for his later role as the aged, wise counsellor in the Trojan War.
The Gorgon's lock, enclosed in a bronze jar, stands for divine protection and concentrated supernatural power.
A hero's child nursed by an animal and found by shepherds echoes the common myth of abandoned heroes' survival.
Entrusting his wife to a centaur known for lust hints at trouble to come and sets up the betrayal.
Nessus presents his revenge as a gift: the supposed love charm is really a means of destroying Hercules.
Hercules is shown as a champion for hire, whose violence is rewarded with land and presented as justice.
The harmless errand for fine clothes quietly anticipates the disaster that follows from the garment brought back.
The reader knows Nessus lied, while Deianira trusts the blood as a love-charm, so her attempt to keep Hercules' love will destroy him.
The hydra, which Hercules once killed, helps kill him through its poison; his own labor comes back against him.
The cloud and thunder lift Hercules from the pyre, signaling that his mortal body is shed and his divine nature recognized.
